title: Steroid Hormone Receptors
terms: Intracellular (cytosolic or nuclear) receptor family; ligand binding turns it into a transcription factor.
C27 starting molecule (S2 figure: polar OH head, rigid planar steroid ring, nonpolar tail); not every steroid-receptor ligand comes from it.
C21; first major stopping point, made "on the way to anywhere"; precursor for testosterone and the corticoids (transcript).
Cholesterol C27; progesterone and corticoids C21; testosterone C19; estradiol C18. Carbons are cleaved along the pathway (transcript).
NOT on slides: primary glucocorticoid in birds and rodents; intermediate toward aldosterone; differs from cortisol by one hydroxyl (transcript).
Adrenal-cortex glucocorticoid; binds BOTH glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors ("key for multiple locks"); about 100x aldosterone concentration (transcript).
"Supercharged" androgen: binds the androgen receptor more readily, at lower concentration, with a bigger effect than testosterone (transcript).
Enzyme converting testosterone to estradiol; testosterone must be present to make estradiol (transcript; not on slides).
Aromatase inhibitor: blocks estradiol formation in endocrine-sensitive cancer (transcript).
Thyroxine (T4), triiodothyronine (T3), reverse T3, retinoic acid (vitamin D3 also pictured) act at this receptor family without being cholesterol-derived.
Prohormone with four iodines; predominant form released by the thyroid; the slide's feedback signal to the pituitary.
Biologically active thyroid hormone; formed by removing one iodine from T4.
Reverse triiodothyronine; inactive form (transcript); listed with the non-cholesterol ligands.
Non-cholesterol agonist of the retinoic acid receptor (nuclear receptor).
Animal form (D3). Transcript: a cholesterol derivative but not a steroid. Agonist of the nuclear vitamin D3 receptor.
Plant form; the S4 structure actually depicts ergocalciferol. D2 vs D3 potency is species dependent (maybe ~1000-fold dosing) - specify which (transcript).
Active vitamin D3: 25-hydroxyl added in the liver, 1-hydroxyl added in the kidney (transcript).
Ligand that binds and activates the receptor.
Ligand that binds the receptor and blocks activation.
What Schultz wants known: testosterone, DHT, estradiol, progesterone, cortisol, aldosterone, vitamin D3, retinoic acid, T3. The drugs are context.
Agonists testosterone, dihydrotestosterone (DHT), nandrolone; antagonists flutamide, enzalutamide.
5-alpha reductase (ENZYME) inhibitor: prostatic hyperplasia, prostate cancer, post-castration; hair growth. Not a receptor blocker (transcript).
Androgen RECEPTOR antagonists; enzalutamide used more in veterinary medicine (transcript). Trap: finasteride hits the enzyme instead.
Anabolic androgen receptor agonist; abuse example: greyhounds dosed with anabolic steroids (transcript).
Agonist estradiol (clomiphene in parentheses); antagonists fulvestrant, tamoxifen.
Agonists cortisol, dexamethasone, prednisolone; antagonist mifepristone. Cytosolic receptor.
Agonist aldosterone; antagonist spironolactone. Cytosolic receptor; drives sodium and water retention.
Agonists vitamin D, maxacalcitol; antagonist ZK159222 (non-clinical). Nuclear receptor.
Agonists retinoic acid, tazarotene; antagonist YCT-529. Nuclear. "Promiscuous": dimerizes with other receptor classes (know that, not the partners).
Agonist T3 (triiodothyronine); no antagonist listed. Nuclear receptor.
Antagonist at BOTH progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors; developed by Roussel, became an abortifacient; shows how hard receptor selectivity is (transcript).
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; also blocks androgen receptors (transcript: used for acne in women, not men).
Bind hydrophobic ligands: protect, add solubility, create a reservoir, greatly extend half-life, smooth swings, reduce renal excretion.
Second carrier for thyroid hormones (with thyroxine binding globulin).
Carrier for steroid androgens and estrogens.
Carries ~75% of cortisol (transcript); lower affinity for progesterone and aldosterone (S16: under 25%; transcript: under 20% of aldosterone).
Low-affinity, high-capacity carrier of hydrophobic molecules: ~50% of aldosterone, ~80% of progesterone (transcript). Listed first for aldosterone (S16).
Ligand (hormone)-binding domain, DNA binding domain, transcription-activating domain; listed as "critical" in the summary.
Binds the specific DNA sequence; Schultz: gives SPECIFICITY to the DNA interaction. Old-exam answer for "which portion is exposed."
Binds co-activator proteins (S8 figure) to start transcription of target genes.
Bound to the ligand-binding domain of the inactive receptor (S8); released when ligand binds (step 4).
Ligand-receptor complex dimerizes, THEN enters the nucleus via the nuclear pore (S10; confirmed in transcript); the dimer binds DNA.
Ligand binds, inhibitory protein released, dimerize, nuclear pore, DNA, co-activators, transcription, RNA out (S9 steps 1-8). Emphasized in class.
DNA site bound by the activated receptor (S19 figure); S8 calls it the receptor-binding element.
Genes activated directly by steroid hormone receptor complexes (S12 figure).
A few early proteins that shut off primary response genes AND turn on secondary response genes.
Later wave: genes switched on by primary response proteins, producing many secondary response proteins.
Examples of primary response proteins (jun, fos on S12; myc added verbally); drive further rounds of RNA synthesis.
Mass-action equilibrium: most bound, some free; only FREE ligand crosses membranes into cells.
Carrier-bound ligand stays in circulation for up to hours, buffering free concentration.
Needs carriers in blood; free form crosses lipid membranes by diffusion.
Slide lists GRIP1, SRC1-3, TRAP, SMRT. Transcript: co-activators AND co-repressors recruited; give cell-type specificity. Names NOT expected.
Signaling mediator for retinoic acid and thyroid hormone receptor (slide expansion).
Hormone is a broadcast signal; a cell responds only with the receptor, needed enzymes (11-beta HSD2, 5-alpha reductase), and co-activators/co-repressors.
Cortisol to cortisone. HSD2: one direction, inactivates cortisol so nephron cells respond to aldosterone. HSD1: both directions (transcript).
Blocks 11-beta HSD, so cortisol occupies the mineralocorticoid receptor: looks like aldosterone excess (transcript).
Converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT); blocked by finasteride (transcript).
Slow: minutes to hours or days; needs transcription and translation.
Requires hormone excretion: conjugation in the liver, then renal excretion.
Mineralocorticoid from the adrenal cortex; released when blood pressure drops; sodium and water retention, potassium excretion.
Renin, then angiotensin, then aldosterone ("goes in that order"). Schultz: "a pathway you better know." Every step has a drug.
Precursor secreted by the LIVER; renin cleaves it to angiotensin I.
Senses decreased renal perfusion and releases renin; increased perfusion INHIBITS renin release (negative feedback, S17).
Enzyme released by the kidney juxtaglomerular apparatus (S17; S18 says macula densa) when renal perfusion falls; angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.
Angiotensin I to angiotensin II; on pulmonary and renal endothelium (S17), mostly in the lungs (transcript); blocked by captopril.
Five effects (S17): sympathetic activity, tubular Na+Cl- reabsorption/K+ excretion, aldosterone secretion, arteriolar vasoconstriction, posterior pituitary ADH secretion.
Angiotensin II receptor (adrenal cortex, vessels, pituitary); cell-surface G protein-coupled receptor via phospholipase C/DAG, plus arrestin (transcript).
Renin inhibitor (blocks angiotensinogen to angiotensin I); spelled A-L-I-S-K-I-R-E-N in class.
ACE inhibitors (block angiotensin I to II); captopril on S18; enalapril likely named verbally ("Anapapril").
AT1R blockers; losartan and valsartan ("biased") on S18; telmisartan likely named verbally ("Telmotran").
Listed beside Na+ retention (S18); Bethany's notes: blocks the Na+ channel. OUTSIDE detail: the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), shown on S19.
Apical Na+ channel (ENaC), apical K+ channel (ROMK), basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase (S19 text; channel names on the figure).
Early aldosterone/MR product (~20 minutes, transcript) that raises apical ENaC and ROMK. Expansion is OUTSIDE.
Apical Na+ channel; more in membrane = Na+ reabsorption; detectable ~2 hours (transcript). Expansion OUTSIDE.
Apical K+ channel for K+ secretion; detectable ~2 hours (transcript). Expansion OUTSIDE.
Removes ENaC from the membrane; SGK1 phosphorylates it, 14-3-3 then holds it, so it cannot remove ENaC.
Binds phosphorylated Nedd4-2 and holds it away from ENaC.
Removes ENaC and ROMK from the membrane; SGK1 inhibits it.
Partners with SGK1 to send ROMK to the membrane.
Repress ENaC transcription; SGK1 relieves the repression.
Trap: RAAS conserves volume (prevents loss, S18) rather than necessarily raising it; thirst adds water (transcript).
Hypothalamic hormone released by cold and stress; reaches anterior pituitary via portal circulation.
Released by pituitary thyrotrophs; stimulates the thyroid to release mostly T4.
Enzymes converting T4 to T3; mainly in kidney and liver.
General increase in metabolism: oxygen consumption, ventilation, thermogenesis, fat and protein mobilization.
Most common endocrine disorder of older cats: weight loss with good appetite, tachycardia, hyperexcitability.
Flame-retardant chemicals suspected as a cause of feline hyperthyroidism.
Most common cause of feline hyperthyroidism; only 2% are adenocarcinoma.
Drug that inhibits T3/T4 production; listed first of three feline treatments (slide spells it Tapazol).
Radio-iodine therapy: beta particles destroy tissue within ~1 mm; half-life 8 days.
Gamma emitter, half-life 13 hours; imaging uptake in thyroid and salivary glands.
Pathway activity is limited by feedback loops (e.g., T4 inhibits TSH release).
traps: Cholesterol derivative vs non-cholesterol ligand: estradiol, testosterone, aldosterone, cortisol, progesterone = cholesterol (S3). T4, T3, reverse T3, retinoic acid (and vitamin D3 pictured) = NOT (S4). Same receptor family, different origin.
Mifepristone blocks TWO receptors: progesterone receptor AND glucocorticoid receptor (S5). Do not pair it with the mineralocorticoid receptor (that is spironolactone).
Cytosolic vs nuclear: glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors = cytosolic; thyroid, vitamin D3, retinoid receptors = nuclear, sitting inactive on DNA (S13).

Cortisol to cortisone = 11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (dehydrogen-ase); testosterone to DHT = 5-alpha reductase; testosterone to estradiol = aromatase (S14, transcript). Do not swap enzyme and substrate.

Renin vs ACE drugs: aliskiren blocks renin (angiotensinogen to angiotensin I); captopril blocks ACE (angiotensin I to II); losartan blocks AT1R; spironolactone blocks the MR; amiloride = Na+ channel (S18).
T4 vs T3: T4 = prohormone, mostly what the thyroid releases, and the slide's feedback signal on TSH; T3 = active hormone made by de-iodinases in kidney and liver (S20, S22).
Iodine isotopes, unit trap: 131I = beta, ~1 mm, half-life 8 days (therapy); 123I = gamma, half-life 13 hours (imaging); 127I = stable (S24).
Aldosterone retains Na+ and water, EXCRETES K+ (S16, S19). Direction flip is the classic trap.
Carriers reduce renal excretion and create a reservoir (S11); termination needs liver conjugation THEN renal excretion (S15). Bound ligand is NOT the active form; free ligand enters cells.
Adenoma vs adenocarcinoma: feline hyperthyroidism is usually a benign adenoma; only 2% are adenocarcinoma (S24).
Cortisol binds the MR too (~100x aldosterone). 11-beta HSD2 = ONE direction, cortisol to inactive cortisone; HSD1 = both directions. Licorice blocks it = fake aldosterone excess (transcript).
Enzyme vs receptor: finasteride blocks the 5-alpha reductase ENZYME; flutamide/enzalutamide block the androgen RECEPTOR (transcript). Letrozole blocks aromatase.
Angiotensinogen comes from the LIVER, not the kidney; the kidney (juxtaglomerular apparatus) releases renin; ACE is mostly in the lungs (S17, transcript).
Blood volume trap: RAAS conserves/manages volume (prevents loss, S18) — Schultz: not necessarily an increase (where would the water come from?).
Timing: SGK1 ~20 minutes (primary); ENaC and ROMK ~2 hours (later) (transcript). Minutes vs hours unit trap.
Spironolactone blocks MR AND androgen receptors; mifepristone blocks progesterone AND glucocorticoid receptors (transcript).

quiz.stem: Which of the following is a cholesterol derivative that acts at an intracellular steroid hormone receptor? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: Aldosterone is on the cholesterol-derivative slide; the other four are the non-cholesterol agonists.

quiz.stem: Which physiological agonist of a 'steroid hormone receptor' is NOT a steroid or cholesterol derivative? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: Retinoic acid is listed with T4, T3 and reverse T3 as a non-cholesterol agonist; the rest are cholesterol derivatives.

quiz.stem: Which molecules are lipid soluble and act through cytosolic or nuclear receptors? (select all that apply)
quiz.why: Testosterone, retinoic acid and vitamin D3 are steroid-receptor ligands (S3-S5, S13). OUTSIDE: ADH and TSH are water-soluble peptides acting at membrane receptors; the slides do not say so.

quiz.stem: Which circulating ligand associates with both transthyretin and thyroxine binding globulin? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: Transthyretin and thyroxine binding globulin carry thyroid hormones.

quiz.stem: Cortisol in plasma is carried mainly by which carrier protein? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: Transcortin carries cortisol, with lower affinity for progesterone and aldosterone.

quiz.stem: After hormone binding, which receptor region must be exposed for the complex to recognize its specific DNA sequence? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: The DNA binding domain binds the specific DNA site; the transcription-activating domain acts after binding.

quiz.stem: Cortisol has bound a cytosolic glucocorticoid receptor and the inhibitory protein has been released. What happens next? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Receptors dimerize and enter the nucleus
bad: Receptors bind DNA at specific sites
RNAs exit the nucleus via pores
quiz.why: Step 4 (inhibitory protein released) is followed by step 5: dimerize and access the nucleus via the nuclear pore. DNA binding is step 6. Transcript confirms: dimerize, then enter via the nuclear pore.

quiz.stem: Which is NOT required for a cell to respond to a steroid hormone? (select one correct response)
bad: The intracellular receptor for that hormone
quiz.why: Specificity requires the receptor, any ancillary enzymes, and the right gene regulatory proteins; no membrane G protein step.

quiz.stem: Which receptors reside inactive on DNA in the nucleus before ligand binding? (select all that apply)
quiz.why: The slide lists thyroid, vitamin D3 and retinoid receptors as nuclear; glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors as cytosolic.

quiz.stem: An epithelial cell has high 11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity, converting cortisol to cortisone. Which naturally occurring molecule increases its expression of an apical Na+ channel, an apical K+ channel and basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: Aldosterone drives transcription of these three transport proteins (S19). Cortisol is ruled out because 11-beta HSD2 converts it to cortisone, which cannot bind the MR (transcript). Spironolactone is a drug.

quiz.stem: In reference to the previous question (high 11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase epithelial cell; Na+ channel, K+ channel and Na+/K+ ATPase upregulated), which receptor mediates this effect? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: Aldosterone acts at the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor; 11-beta HSD2 keeps cortisol off it (transcript).

quiz.stem: A newly discovered molecule, Kansatrol, has a large positive logP (octanol/water partition coefficient), circulates bound to a carrier protein, and activates a cytosolic receptor. Which real molecule does it most resemble? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: OUTSIDE: high logP = lipid soluble. Lipid soluble ligands need carriers (S11); cortisol's glucocorticoid receptor is cytosolic, while T3, retinoic acid and vitamin D3 receptors are nuclear (S13).

quiz.stem: New hormone alpha is water soluble; new hormone beta is lipid soluble and carrier-bound. Which statement is correct? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Beta has the larger reservoir and slower termination
bad: Alpha has the larger reservoir and slower termination
Beta circulates mostly free and is cleared rapidly
Alpha needs a carrier protein to stay in plasma
Beta acts faster because it crosses membranes
quiz.why: Carrier binding creates a vascular reservoir, reduces renal excretion and slows the time course.

quiz.stem: Which drug-target pairing matches the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone slide? (select one correct response)
bad: Captopril blocks the angiotensin II receptor
quiz.why: Aliskiren = renin; captopril = ACE; losartan = AT1R; spironolactone = mineralocorticoid receptor.

quiz.stem: Per the slides, which extracellular signal inhibits thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) release from the anterior pituitary? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: S22 states T4 exerts negative feedback on TSH release. Textbooks emphasize T3 (see flag); use the slide.

quiz.stem: An older cat has weight loss despite a good appetite, tachycardia, hyperexcitability and a poor hair coat; plasma thyroxine (T4) is high. What is the most likely cause? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: Feline hyperthyroidism is most often a thyroid adenoma; only 2% are adenocarcinoma.

quiz.stem: Which statements about iodine isotopes in feline thyroid disease are correct? (select all that apply)
ok: Iodine-131 emits beta particles destroying tissue within ~1 mm
Iodine-123 emits gamma rays and is used for scintigraphy
bad: Iodine-127 is the radioactive isotope used for treatment
Iodine-131 has a half-life of about 13 hours
Iodine-123 has a half-life of about 8 days
quiz.why: 131I: beta, ~1 mm, 8 days (therapy). 123I: gamma, 13 hours (imaging). 127I is stable.

quiz.stem: Mifepristone (RU-486) is listed as an antagonist at which pair of receptors? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: The ligand table lists mifepristone under both the progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors.

quiz.stem: A hypertensive dog receives a drug that blocks conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I. Which drug was given? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: Aliskiren = renin; captopril = ACE; losartan = AT1R; spironolactone = MR; amiloride = Na+ channel.

quiz.stem: In the S19 aldosterone-sensitive cell, how does SGK1 increase apical ENaC? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Phosphorylates Nedd4-2 so it cannot remove ENaC
bad: Dephosphorylates Nedd4-2 so it removes ENaC faster
Activates WNK4 so it inserts more ENaC channels
Binds the hormone response element to repress ENaC
Phosphorylates NHERF2 so it removes ROMK channels
quiz.why: SGK1 phosphorylates Nedd4-2 (held by 14-3-3), inhibits WNK4, sends ENaC to the membrane, and relieves Dot1/AF9 repression.

quiz.stem: Which are effects of angiotensin II on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone diagram? (select all that apply)
ok: Aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex
Antidiuretic hormone secretion from the posterior pituitary
bad: Renin release from the juxtaglomerular apparatus
quiz.why: Angiotensin II's five arrows: sympathetic activity, tubular Na+Cl- reabsorption/K+ excretion, aldosterone, vasoconstriction, ADH. Renin is upstream and is inhibited by increased perfusion; angiotensinogen comes from the liver.

quiz.stem: A dog eats a large amount of black licorice, which blocks 11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase in nephron cells. Which outcome is expected? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Cortisol occupies the MR, mimicking aldosterone excess
bad: Cortisone accumulates and activates the MR directly
Aldosterone synthesis by the adrenal cortex stops entirely
Cortisol is converted to cortisone faster than normal
Mineralocorticoid receptor expression is lost in the nephron
quiz.why: 11-beta HSD2 normally inactivates cortisol (~100x aldosterone) so the MR responds only to aldosterone; blocking it lets cortisol activate the MR.

quiz.stem: A dog with prostatic hyperplasia needs the androgen receptor itself blocked, not DHT synthesis. Which drug fits? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: Finasteride blocks the 5-alpha reductase enzyme; enzalutamide (and flutamide) block the androgen receptor; letrozole blocks aromatase; mifepristone and tamoxifen act at other receptors.

quiz.stem: Letrozole is used for an endocrine-sensitive cancer. Which conversion does it block? (select one correct response)
quiz.why: Letrozole blocks aromatase (testosterone to estradiol). 5-alpha reductase makes DHT; 11-beta HSD makes cortisone.

quiz.stem: Aldosterone reaches a collecting duct cell at time zero. Per lecture, when do newly made SGK1 and ENaC/ROMK become detectable? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: SGK1 ~20 minutes; ENaC and ROMK ~2 hours
bad: ENaC and ROMK ~20 minutes; SGK1 ~2 hours
SGK1 ~20 hours; ENaC and ROMK ~2 days
SGK1, ENaC and ROMK all at ~20 minutes
SGK1 ~2 minutes; ENaC and ROMK ~20 minutes
quiz.why: SGK1 is an early (primary) product, ~20 minutes; ENaC and ROMK come later, ~2 hours (transcript).

quiz.stem: After moderate fluid loss, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system drives renal salt retention and ADH-mediated water retention. Per Dr. Schultz, what best describes the effect on blood volume? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Volume is conserved by preventing further loss
bad: Volume rises well above the starting baseline
Volume falls because arterioles are constricted
Volume is unchanged because sodium is excreted
Volume rises because water leaves the cells
quiz.why: S18: conserves blood volume. Schultz: not necessarily increased (where would the water come from?), it is managed; drinking adds water. S17's 'effective circulating volume increases' — see flag.

flags: Lecture number: LC23 vs LC25
Title slide (S1) and Canvas file say "LC23"; 2026 schedule numbers it LC25 (Cell Signaling 3, Fri 10/23/2026) · use LC25.
Slide typo: Dexamathasone
S5 spells "Dexamathasone" · correct spelling is dexamethasone; use that.
Slide typo: Enzolutamide
S5 spells "Enzolutamide" · correct spelling is enzalutamide; use that.
Slide typo: Reinoic acid
S5 spells "Reinoic Acid" · means retinoic acid.
T4 as an 'agonist': S4 vs S5

S4 lists T4, T3 and reverse T3 as steroid-receptor agonists; S5 lists only T3 as the thyroid hormone receptor agonist, and S22 calls T3 the biologically active form · use T3 as the receptor agonist; T4 counts as a non-cholesterol ligand for S4-type questions.
Clomiphene in parentheses

S5 lists clomiphene in parentheses under estrogen receptor agonists · OUTSIDE: it is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (mixed agonist/antagonist) — confirm. For now: estrogen receptor ligand, agonist column.
11-beta HSD role (CLOSED)
S14 lists cortisol to cortisone; transcript adds 11-beta HSD2 (one direction) keeps cortisol off the MR so nephron cells respond to aldosterone; HSD1 is bidirectional; licorice blocks it · CLOSED.
Vitamin D3 origin: S4 vs transcript

S4 places vitamin D3 under "Not cholesterol derivatives" (image: drawn beside cholesterol, opened ring). Transcript: vitamin D3 IS a cholesterol derivative but NOT a steroid; S4 structure is actually ergocalciferol (D2). 2023 exam used vitamin D3 as a distractor for "cholesterol derivative" · use: cholesterol derivative, not a steroid; if a classic steroid is offered, pick it.
Sex-steroid receptor location not stated

S13 places only GR/MR (cytosolic) and thyroid/vitamin D3/retinoid (nuclear); androgen, estrogen, progesterone receptors are not placed. The 2025 past-question answer (17-beta estradiol for 'cytosolic receptor') was written from earlier lectures, not an official key · OUTSIDE: textbooks call the estrogen receptor mostly nuclear. Use only the S13 lists for now; confirm with transcript.
Co-activator names not tested

S13 expansions (SRC, GRIP1, SMRT) differ from textbooks (OUTSIDE: SMRT is a co-repressor). Transcript: "I don't expect you to know these co-factors," only that co-activators AND co-repressors exist and give cell-type specificity · do not memorize names.
Step count: S9 vs S10 (RESOLVED)

Checked against slide image: S9 figure numbers 1-8 match S10 steps 1-8 (1 hormone in blood, 2 bound to carriers, 3 free hormone into cytosol, 4 receptor binds, 5 complex enters nucleus through nuclear pore, 6 binds DNA with co-factor, 7 RNA transcribed, 8 RNA exits nuclear pore). S10 steps 9-10 (protein synthesis, change in function) are not drawn. No conflict; learn the 10-step S10 list.
Dimerization order: S10 vs S11 (RESOLVED)

Transcript: the ligand-receptor complex dimerizes, THEN enters the nucleus via the nuclear pore; he notes S9 does not draw the dimerization · use S10 order. Nuclear receptors already sit on DNA (S13).
Aldosterone carriers
S6 lists transcortin (lower affinity for aldosterone) but not albumin; S16 lists albumin plus transcortin (less than 25%) · use S16 for aldosterone.
Renin source: S17 vs S18

S17 figure: renin released by the kidney on decreased renal perfusion (juxtaglomerular apparatus). S18 text: "(macula densa)" — part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus. Transcript: juxtaglomerular apparatus senses pressure and releases renin · answer "juxtaglomerular apparatus." OUTSIDE: juxtaglomerular (granular) cells secrete; macula densa senses NaCl.
Feedback signal: T4 vs T3

S22: T4 inhibits TSH release from the pituitary · OUTSIDE: textbooks emphasize T3 (local T4-to-T3 conversion). Past questions (answers not official keys): 2023 asked for one signal, 2024 offered 'T4 and/or T3'. Use the slide: T4; pick 'T4 and/or T3' if that is the option.
S19 word order
S19 says aldosterone causes "translation and transcription" · real order is transcription then translation (S10, S11).
Channel names (ENaC, ROMK, SGK1) — on the S19 figure

Checked against slide image: ENaC, ROMK, SGK1, Nedd4-2, 14-3-3, WNK4, NHERF2, Dot1/AF9 and HRE are labeled on the S19 figure, and the transcript uses ENaC and ROMK · know the names. Only the expansions (epithelial sodium channel, renal outer medullary potassium channel, serum- and glucocorticoid-regulated kinase 1) are OUTSIDE.
Brand name typo
S24 says "Tapazol" · US brand is Tapazole (OUTSIDE, confirm).
Old-exam items vs this deck
Finasteride is now covered verbally (blocks 5-alpha reductase). "TSH receptor = 7 transmembrane, Gs" is still LC27 content, not this deck · OUTSIDE for LC25.
Drug annotations (amiloride, "biased" valsartan)

S18 lists amiloride beside Na+ retention and valsartan as "biased" without mechanism; transcript does not explain either · Bethany's notes: amiloride = Na+ channel. OUTSIDE: amiloride blocks ENaC; "biased" = biased agonism at AT1R.
Carrier percentage: S16 vs transcript
S16: transcortin carries "less than 25%" of aldosterone. Transcript: "a little less than 20%"; ~50% on albumin · use the slide number (less than 25%) if asked; know albumin carries more.
Blood volume wording: S17 vs S18 vs transcript

S17 figure: "effective circulating volume increases." S18: RAAS "conserves blood volume." Transcript: not necessarily increasing volume, preventing loss; "manages blood volume" · use conserve/maintain; avoid "volume increases" unless the stem quotes S17.
Drug scope: memorize or not?

Bethany heard "memorize the pathway and the drugs." Auto-transcript: "Do I want you to know all those drugs...? No, but..." then a student asks what blocks renin (aliskiren, spelled out) · unclear. Safe plan: know ONE drug per step (aliskiren, captopril/enalapril, losartan/telmisartan, spironolactone, amiloride).
Lecture coverage
Transcript covers S1-S19 only; thyroid (S20-S24) and summary (S25) not yet lectured · thyroid content is slides-only until that transcript arrives.
